title: Only Happens Here: 10 Traditions That Make No Sense Anywhere Else
description: From signing historic books to cracking lobster claws, explore the unique rituals and long-standing traditions that define the Bowdoin College experience.

cards.title: Signing the Matriculation Book
cards.subtitle: A permanent mark in college history
cards.notes: Visit the President's Office during orientation to sign the historic matriculation book, joining a lineage of alumni that includes Nathaniel Hawthorne and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.
cards.short_summary: First-year students officially join the college community by signing a historic ledger in the President's Office.
cards.evidence_claim: The tradition involves first-year students visiting the president's office to sign matriculation books, a practice that has been documented with volumes dating back to the college's early history.
cards.source_title: Students Add Their Names to Bowdoin's History
cards.access_notes: Occurs annually during Orientation for incoming first-year students.

cards.title: The Orientation Lobster Bake
cards.subtitle: A quintessential Maine welcome
cards.notes: Head to Farley Fields after Convocation to enjoy a traditional Maine lobster dinner with the entire campus community to kick off the academic year.
cards.short_summary: An annual outdoor feast featuring over 1,500 lobsters to welcome students back to campus in the fall.
cards.evidence_claim: The Lobster Bake has opened the academic year since the 1960s and serves as a bookend tradition, with another bake held at Commencement.
cards.source_title: From sea to stomach: A peek into Lobster Bake logistics
cards.access_notes: Held on Farley Fields; open to the Bowdoin campus community.

cards.title: The Bowdoin Hello
cards.subtitle: Campus-wide culture of greeting
cards.notes: Practice the friendly habit of saying 'hello' to everyone you pass on the campus paths, a tradition rooted in 1960s fraternity culture.
cards.short_summary: A long-standing social norm where students and faculty greet one another while walking across the small campus.
cards.evidence_claim: The 'Bowdoin Hello' is a recognized campus tradition where students greet each other on paths, originating from 1960s fraternity pledge requirements.
cards.access_notes: An informal daily practice across all campus walkways.

cards.title: Ivies Weekend
cards.subtitle: Spring's historic rite of passage
cards.notes: Celebrate the end of winter with concerts and outdoor events during this multi-day festival, which evolved from an 1865 ivy-planting ceremony.
cards.short_summary: A major spring festival featuring live music and social events, originally centered on planting ivy at the Chapel.
cards.evidence_claim: Ivies began as 'Ivy Day' in 1865 with the planting of ivy at the Chapel and has evolved into a weekend-long spring celebration.
cards.source_title: The Root of Ivies | Bowdoin College
cards.access_notes: Held annually in late April or early May; specific event locations vary.

cards.title: Luck of the Polar Bear
cards.subtitle: A granite mascot for good fortune
cards.notes: Visit the life-sized granite polar bear statue in front of Sargent Gym, a gift from the Class of 1912 that serves as a campus icon.
cards.short_summary: A historic granite statue of the college mascot, often visited by students for luck or photos.
cards.evidence_claim: The life-size granite polar bear statue was designed by Frederic George Richard Roth and presented to the college in 1937.
cards.source_title: The Bowdoin Bear | Peary-MacMillan Arctic Museum
cards.access_notes: Located outdoors in front of the Peter Buck Center for Health and Fitness/Sargent Gym.

cards.title: Sarah and James Bowdoin Day
cards.subtitle: Honoring academic excellence
cards.notes: Attend the fall ceremony in Pickard Theater where the top 20 percent of students are recognized as scholars and awarded historic bookplates.
cards.short_summary: An annual academic convocation that honors high-achieving students with the title of Bowdoin Scholar.
cards.evidence_claim: The ceremony recognizes the top 20 percent of students by GPA and includes the presentation of Book Awards featuring a replica college bookplate.
cards.source_title: Students Urged to Maintain an Open Mind on Sarah and James Bowdoin Day
cards.access_notes: Held annually in October in the Pickard Theater, Memorial Hall.

cards.title: Common Good Day
cards.subtitle: Service as a core value
cards.notes: Join hundreds of classmates for a day of community service in the Brunswick area, honoring President Joseph McKeen's 1802 charge.
cards.short_summary: A campus-wide day of service where students, faculty, and staff volunteer at local non-profits and community sites.
cards.evidence_claim: Common Good Day is an annual event organized by the McKeen Center, rooted in the college's founding mission to serve the common good.
cards.source_title: The Joseph McKeen Center for the Common Good
cards.access_notes: Typically held on a Saturday in September.

cards.title: Winter Weekend Snow Sculptures
cards.subtitle: Icy art on the quad
cards.notes: Watch or participate in the snow sculpture competition on the quad, a tradition that has seen massive polar bears and creative designs since 1945.
cards.short_summary: A winter festival featuring snow carving, ice skating, and outdoor activities to celebrate the Maine winter.
cards.evidence_claim: Winter Weekend includes a long-standing snow sculpture tradition documented in the Orient archives since at least 1945.
cards.source_title: Buried under history: Revisiting Bowdoin's Winter's Weekend snow sculpture tradition
cards.access_notes: Held annually in February on the Main Quad.

cards.title: Dinner with Six Strangers
cards.subtitle: Breaking bread with new faces
cards.notes: Sign up for a meal hosted by faculty or staff to meet five other students you've never met, fostering community through conversation.
cards.short_summary: A residential life program that brings together small groups of students who are strangers for a shared meal.
cards.evidence_claim: The 'Dinner with Six Strangers' program is a recognized tradition aimed at bringing together people on campus who may not otherwise interact.
cards.access_notes: Requires sign-up through Residential Life; locations vary by host.

cards.title: The Whispering Pines
cards.subtitle: A symbolic sprig for graduates
cards.notes: Wear a sprig of pine during the Baccalaureate ceremony, a tradition honoring the 'Whispering Pines' that have symbolized the college since 1806.
cards.short_summary: Graduating seniors wear pine sprigs to honor the college's historic connection to the Maine wilderness.
cards.evidence_claim: The pine tree is a central symbol of Bowdoin, with the Peucinian Society adopting the 'whispering pines' motto in 1806 and sprigs used in ceremonies.
